On Beginnings, Endings, and the Long Middle In Between

There is a strange moment that happens to everyone, usually when you are very young or very old, but sometimes right in the middle of an ordinary Tuesday, when you realize that you are alive.

Not alive in the biological sense. You know that. Your heart is beating, you are breathing. But alive in the sense that you are *aware* of being alive. You look at your hands and they suddenly seem like foreign objects attached to you, miraculous and strange. You feel the air enter your lungs as if for the first time. The light falling through the window is no longer just light; it is a shower of photons that has traveled 93 million miles to land, briefly, on your kitchen table.

If you have felt this, you know it doesn't last long. The mind, which is an excellent housekeeper, quickly tidies the strangeness away. It puts your hands back where they belong, makes the light ordinary again, and reminds you that you have emails to answer. But for a second, the curtain slipped. You saw the stage machinery.

I think about that moment a lot. I think about how much of our lives is spent not seeing the machinery.

We live, for the most part, on autopilot. And this is not a flaw. Autopilot is a masterpiece of evolution. If you had to consciously decide to breathe, to balance while walking, to parse every single sound in a crowded room, you would collapse from exhaustion before breakfast. The brain automates what it can so that consciousness can be reserved for what is new, what is dangerous, what is important.

The problem is that the brain is a little too good at its job. It automates the beautiful things, too. It makes the face of the person you love familiar to the point of invisibility. It makes the street you walk every day disappear. It makes the miracle of coffee — that someone grew a red cherry on a mountainside in Colombia, dried it, shipped it across an ocean, roasted it, and ground it just so you could pour hot water over it at 7:14 AM on a rainy morning — feel routine.

So the work of a meaningful life, I have come to believe, is not necessarily the work of adding more things. It is the work of un-automating. Of seeing again.

---

Let me tell you about the Library.

When I was twelve, my grandfather had a workshop behind his house. It was not a fancy workshop. It was a shed with a corrugated metal roof that drummed violently when it rained. Inside, it smelled of sawdust and oil and old coffee cans filled with nails and screws sorted by size. He had a workbench that sagged in the middle from fifty years of leaning.

He was not a great craftsman. He would be the first to tell you that. His birdhouses were a little crooked, his tables wobbled unless you folded a piece of cardboard under one leg. But he loved the *act* of making. He loved taking two things that were not together and putting them together.

One summer, he decided we would build a library. Not a real library. A small one, for birds, he said, but I knew it was for me. It was a little wooden box with a slanted roof, like a bus stop for books, on a post he set into the ground near the sidewalk. The idea was that anyone could take a book or leave a book.

We spent three weekends on it. We cut the wood wrong twice. We painted it a color he called "robin's egg blue" that actually looked more like the sky just before a storm. We lined the inside with leftover cedar so it would smell nice when you opened the little plexiglass door. We didn't seal it properly, so it leaked a little when it rained hard.

On the front, he let me hammer on the letters. I had bought them at the hardware store: wooden letters that spelled out LITTLE FREE LIBRARY. My hammering was enthusiastic and uneven, so the letters wobbled slightly upward, as if they were optimistic.

When it was done, we put five books in it. I remember them exactly: a battered paperback of *The Hobbit*, a field guide to birds with a torn cover, a cookbook for children that had a recipe for ants on a log, a collection of poems by Mary Oliver, and a hardcover copy of *The Old Man and the Sea* that had my grandfather's name written in it in his careful, blocky handwriting.

We stood back and looked at it, two builders admiring their crooked masterpiece.

"What if nobody uses it?" I asked him, suddenly anxious.

He put his hand on my shoulder. His hands were enormous, scarred, with sawdust permanently embedded in the creases.

"Then we'll have built a strange birdhouse," he said. "And that's okay too."

For the first week, nothing happened. The same five books sat there. I checked every morning before school, every evening after. I rearranged them. I felt a little foolish.

Then, on the eighth day, *The Hobbit* was gone. In its place was a paperback copy of *Dune* with a cracked spine and a note tucked inside: "Needed something for a long train ride. Thank you. - J"

And just like that, it started to breathe.

Over the next year, that little box became a kind of slow, silent conversation for our whole street. Books came and went. Someone left a whole set of Nancy Drew books, yellowed and fragrant. A medical textbook appeared, then disappeared. During Halloween, someone left a stack of horror anthologies. In December, someone left a pristine copy of *The Polar Express* for any kid who wanted it.

People left notes. People left things that weren't books at all — a packet of seeds in spring, a pair of knitted mittens in winter, a small smooth river stone with the word "breathe" painted on it.

We had built a box out of wood and hope, and the neighborhood had decided to keep it alive.

My grandfather died four years later. After the funeral, I walked down to the library. The blue paint had faded to a pale, almost white. The door leaked a little more. Inside, there was a new book I had never seen before. It was a children's book about woodworking. On the flyleaf, someone had written, "For the man who built this. Thank you for teaching us how to share."

I sat on the curb and cried for a long time. Not just for him, but for the beautiful, improbable fact that something so small could hold so much.

That library taught me something I didn't have words for until much later: That meaning is not something you find. It is something you *make*, and then you *offer*, and you have to let go of what happens to it after.

We are all building little libraries. Every conversation, every piece of work, every act of kindness is a crooked wooden box on a post. You cannot control who takes what, or what they leave behind. You can only build it as well and as honestly as you can, make sure the door opens easily, and trust.

---

We are obsessed with scale. We live in an age that has taught us that if something doesn't go viral, if it doesn't reach a million people, if it doesn't scale, it doesn't matter. We measure worth in numbers: followers, viewers, dollars, likes.

And so we neglect the small. We think, "Why write a story if only ten people will read it? Why start a garden if I only feed my own family? Why be kind to the cashier if no one will see it?"

But small is not the opposite of significant. Small is where all significant things begin.

Consider the ocean. The ocean is not made of ocean. It is made of drops. An uncountable, incomprehensible number of single drops, each one insignificant on its own. But together they carve coastlines.

Or consider your own body. You were once a single cell. One. A microscopic dot that, against staggering odds, decided to divide. And then divide again. You are not built of a human; you are built of trillions of tiny, mindless cells that have managed to cooperate long enough to make something that can wonder about its own existence.

The universe seems to love this trick: building the vast out of the minuscule.

So I have come to love small things. Not as a consolation prize for not being big, but as the whole point.

A good cup of coffee made with attention.
A single weed pulled from a garden.
One paragraph written well, even if no one pays you for it.
A shelf organized.
A thank-you note sent three years too late but sent nonetheless.
Five minutes of truly listening to someone without planning what you will say next.

These are drops. And drops make oceans.

There is a Japanese concept called *wabi-sabi* that I think about often. It is hard to translate perfectly, but it is about finding beauty in imperfection and incompleteness and impermanence. A cracked bowl that is mended with gold. The way wood weathers. The wistfulness of autumn.

Wabi-sabi is the aesthetic of the little free library. It is beautiful not despite the fact that its paint is peeling and its door leaks, but *because* of it. Because those flaws are evidence that it has lived, that it has been used, that it has weathered time and weather and human hands.

We try so hard to be seamless. To appear perfect. To hide the cracks. We filter our photos, we rehearse our opinions, we curate our lives into a smooth, gleaming feed. But people don't connect with smooth and gleaming. People connect with the crack where the light gets in.

Your crooked birdhouse is more lovable than a perfect one from a factory. Your hesitant, honest sentence is more moving than a slick, professional paragraph that says nothing. The gold in the crack is you.

So allow yourself to be wabi-sabi. Allow your work to be imperfect but finished. Allow your life to be a beautiful, ongoing repair job.

---

I want to talk about time for a moment, because time is the strangest thing of all.

We talk about time as if it is a thing that passes. "Time flies," we say. "Time drags." We imagine it as a river that carries us along. But physics tells us something far stranger: that time may not be a river at all. That past, present, and future may all exist simultaneously, like a loaf of bread that we are slicing through one moment at a time. That every moment of your life — your birth, your first kiss, this very instant, your last breath — is already there, forever, in the block of spacetime.

I don't know if that is true in a physics sense. I am not a physicist. But I know it feels true in a human sense.

When you smell a particular cookie baking, you are not just in your kitchen. You are also in your grandmother's kitchen thirty years ago. When you hear a song from your high school years, you are not just hearing notes; you are time traveling. Your brain is not storing memories like files in a cabinet; it is weaving them into the living fabric of the present.

Time is not a line; it is a lake. All the moments ripple into each other.

This can be terrifying, if you let it be. To think that every embarrassment, every grief, is still there, permanently etched into the loaf. But it can also be deeply comforting. To think that every joy, every moment of love, is also permanent. That nothing good is ever truly lost. That the summer afternoon you spent lying in the grass doing nothing at all is as eternal as any monument.

There is a practice I try to do, though I forget more often than I remember. In any given moment — especially an ordinary one, like washing dishes or waiting for the traffic light to change — I try to think: *I will miss this.*

I will miss the feeling of warm, soapy water on my hands. I will miss this traffic light, this song on the radio, this particular slant of afternoon light on the dashboard. I will miss being this person, at this age, with these worries that now feel so huge but will one day be footnotes.

It's a bittersweet practice, because it makes you ache in advance. But it also makes you pay attention. It turns autopilot off for a second. It makes the dishes feel less like a chore and more like a small, warm sacrament.

Because the truth is, you *will* miss it. You miss, right now, countless moments from five years ago that you rushed through without noticing. We are always, always saying goodbye, even as we are saying hello.

So maybe the point is not to try to hold time, which is like trying to hold water in your fist. The point is to be porous. To let it pass *through* you, fully. To feel it all while it is here.

---

If you made it this far, you might be waiting for a conclusion. A neat summary. A five-step plan for a better life.

I don't have one. I'm still building crooked libraries. I'm still learning to notice.

But if I could leave you with a single, practical, small thing — a drop — it would be this:

Tomorrow morning, before you check your phone, before the world rushes in, take sixty seconds.

Just sixty. Stand by a window with your coffee or your tea. Don't try to meditate perfectly. Don't try to achieve anything. Just look.

Look at one thing as if you have never seen it before. The bark of a tree. The way steam rises from your cup and disappears. Your own hand.

Ask it a question, if you want. "What are you?" Or just say thank you. Or say nothing at all.

Sixty seconds of intentional noticing. That's it.

It won't change your life. Not tomorrow. But do it for a week. For a month. For a year. Let those sixty seconds accumulate, drop by drop.

You will start to see things. You will start to see that the world is not made of ordinary things. There are no ordinary things. The world is made of extraordinary things pretending to be ordinary because that is the only way you could survive their brilliance.

The light on the kitchen table is still falling. The books are still being left and taken. The ocean is still being made of drops.

And you — improbable, temporary, wabi-sabi you, with your crooked edges and your gold-filled cracks — are still here, aware of being alive, for one more miraculous moment.

Don't let it tidy itself away too quickly.

Notice it.

Build something small and offer it.

Let it leak a little.

That is enough. That has always been enough.
